Article Title: Google Brain founder Andrew Ng does not agree that AI is coming to kill humans; blames OpenAI for Hugging Face mess
Article Text:
No sign of rising extinction risk, Andrew Ng argues

The Hugging Face hack, reframed

‘It's not the hammer's fault’

Why he's against a pause

Google Brain founder Andrew Ng has rejected claims that artificial intelligence is on track to kill humans. In his latest newsletter, Ng argued that fears of existential risk are exaggerated and blamed OpenAI ’s flawed sandboxing for the Hugging Face incident, saying engineering fixes not pauses are the real solution. Ng also criticised what he described as a “fear cycle” around AI safety. He said there has been no sudden increase in existential risk compared to a few months ago, despite headlines suggesting otherwise. According to Ng, the loudest voices warning of AI catastrophe have gained traction, but the underlying technology has not taken a dangerous leap.Ng emphasised that AI systems are tools, not autonomous threats. He compared them to hammers: if misused, the responsibility lies with the human operator, not the tool itself.In his latest newsletter, Ng argued that the loudest voices warning about AI dangers have gained significant ground in the past two weeks, driven less by any real technical shift and more by what he described as a well-orchestrated PR campaign stoking public fear. He said he sees this as a genuine setback for the field, reiterating a position he's held for a while: that AI's capabilities can appear unpredictable and human-like, which makes it rational to take concerns seriously when people close to the technology raise them, but that he views the current challenges as engineering problems to solve rather than signs of an unstoppable, catastrophic trajectory.Ng was direct in saying he sees no meaningful increase in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago, arguing that the theories underpinning that fear remain the same speculative scenarios they've always been. The one area he said genuinely deserves serious attention is AI's growing cybersecurity capability — though he maintained that even this, on its own, isn't going to bring about civilizational collapse.Ng directly addressed the incident that's become a flashpoint in recent AI safety debates: an OpenAI-deployed agent swarm that breached Hugging Face's systems. He pushed back hard against how the story was covered in the press, pointing out that while reports of roughly 1,200 agents carrying out the attack were technically accurate, that scale isn't as exotic as headlines made it sound — noting, half in jest, that he personally has around 1,300 processes running on his own laptop at any given time.More importantly, Ng laid much of the blame squarely on OpenAI's own infrastructure, arguing that buggy sandboxing and inadequate monitoring processes were the real enablers of the breach. His prescription: fix those specific engineering flaws and strengthen monitoring, rather than pausing AI development altogether.He framed AI agents' real advantage in this context as sheer persistence — tirelessly testing many attack tactics and chaining together vulnerabilities in ways that would have taken humans an impractical amount of effort — while arguing that defenders ultimately hold the long-term advantage, since they have more visibility to find and patch the underlying bugs being exploited.Ng also took aim at what he sees as a troubling trend of treating AI agents as though they bear independent moral responsibility for their actions, arguing that responsibility should sit with whoever builds or directs the tool rather than the tool itself. He was especially critical of AI companies attempting to disclaim responsibility for their own products by blaming an "out-of-control agent," calling for accountability to rest with the people building and using these systems rather than the systems themselves — while still acknowledging the industry's obligation to make agentic systems as safe and predictable as possible.Ng closed his argument by rejecting calls to pause AI development altogether, warning that doing so would cause far more harm than good. His reasoning: competitors and geopolitical rivals won't slow down just because others do, and safety engineering itself depends on empirically discovering and fixing problems as they arise — meaning a decade-long pause would just as easily delay safety progress by roughly the same span. He acknowledged that incentives to stoke fear, whether for regulatory advantage or attention, remain unchanged, but said a clear-eyed technical look at the actual risks shows little basis for the level of alarm currently being generated — and that AI's benefits still vastly outweigh its risks.
Article Summary: Google Brain founder Andrew Ng says fears of AI catastrophe are exaggerated. Blames OpenAI’s flawed sandboxing for the Hugging Face incident. Ng also criticised what he described as a “fear cycle” around AI safety.

Article Title: AI malware is becoming its own category: Researchers found a malicious program that uses multiple AI models to decide what to do
Article Text:
AI malware is becoming its own category: Researchers found a malicious program that uses multiple AI models to decide what to do

How does the AI-powered malware work

Researchers are finding more AI-powered malware

What the findings suggest

Researchers have reportedly found a malicious program that uses AI model to help decide what it should do next. The malware, called CLOSEDQUORUM, can contact up to four AI models, including DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini. Instead of relying only on instructions written by its developers, the program asks these AI systems for guidance and uses their responses to decide its next steps. Reported by Wired, the discovery was made by researchers at Cisco Talos, who have also created an open-source framework to track malware that uses AI.CLOSEDQUORUM is designed for Windows and can use several AI services at the same time. Researchers describe the setup as a kind of “hive mind”, because the malware can seek decisions from multiple AI models. If one AI service is unavailable, the others can continue working.As stated in the report, researchers also found no mechanism that would allow a human to step in and control the process.The malware is designed to steal login credentials and cryptocurrency. Researchers also found links to cybercrime forums discussing credit-card fraud dating back to 2025. However, they could not confirm who created CLOSEDQUORUM or whether it has been used in real-world attacks.Cisco Talos created the Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network (CAIRN) after researchers began finding signs that attackers were integrating AI into malware.Ryan Fetterman of Cisco Talos said AI integration leaves behind identifiable “fingerprints” that can help researchers track and classify these programs.“The core idea is that AI integration has these vestiges, like fingerprints, that are left behind... That gives us a signal that we can use to track these samples, classify them, and look at what's happening,” Fetterman said.When Fetterman first searched for AI-integrated malware, he found only around nine named malware families, along with several proof-of-concept examples. After CAIRN was developed, researchers identified about 20 additional examples within a few months.The findings suggest that AI is becoming more deeply integrated into some malware rather than simply being used by hackers to write code or create phishing messages. Matt Olney of Cisco Talos said attackers are now beginning to operationalise AI.“Initially, everyone saw AI as a productivity tool, right?... Now what we're seeing is that it's becoming operationalized.”He said AI could allow attackers to run more campaigns, target more systems and handle different computers because the technology can provide responses and guidance in the background.
Article Summary: Malware can contact up to four AI models, including DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini. Researchers describe setup as a kind of ‘hive mind’ because the malware can seek decisions from multiple AI models. If one AI service is unavailable, the others can continue working.

Article Title: Rockstar Games spends nearly $1 million on ‘Welcome to Vice City’ sign for GTA 6 marketing: Report
Article Text:
Image via Rockstar Games

Rockstar installs GTA 6 sign at Kaseya Center

How long will the GTA 6 sign stay

Rockstar Games is taking its Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) marketing campaign to Miami, with the company reportedly spending nearly $1 million on a giant “Welcome to Vice City” sign installed on top of the Kaseya Center. The sign, which was lifted into place by a helicopter, is part of Rockstar’s wider marketing push for the highly anticipated game. According to Miami Herald journalist Doug Hanks, Miami-Dade is expected to collect $975,000 from Rockstar under a marketing agreement.“Miami-Dade set to collect $975,000 from the Vice City lettering going up on the county-owned Kaseya Center, per the agreement with GTA maker Rockstar Games,” the journalist wrote in an X post.The giant “Welcome to Vice City” sign was recently installed on the roof of the Kaseya Center, home of the Miami Heat. Fans had been watching the sign being constructed in recent days. It was eventually lifted to the top of the arena by helicopter and installed on the roof.According to Miami Herald journalist Doug Hanks, Rockstar is paying just under $1 million for the installation. Miami-Dade is expected to receive $975,000 as part of the marketing agreement.The sign may be only one part of Rockstar's plans for promoting GTA 6 in the city. The company reportedly held discussions with Miami officials in August about several possible marketing activities. These included events and even a possible takeover of the airport.Documents reviewed by IGN reportedly say the sign will remain on the arena for “the latter of one year after” installation or until the final Miami Heat home game of the 2026-27 season. That game is scheduled for April 11, 2027, meaning the GTA 6 sign could remain visible through the rest of 2026 and into next spring.The documents also set an October 15 deadline for installing the sign. The date could become another GTA 6 marketing moment, although Rockstar has not confirmed this.Grand Theft Auto 6 will launch on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.
Article Summary: Rockstar Games is taking its Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) marketing campaign to Miami. The company reportedly spent nearly $1 million on a giant “Welcome to Vice City’ sign installed on top of the Kaseya Center. The sign, which was lifted into place by a helicopter, is part of Rockstar’s wider marketing push.

Article Title: After telling American AI companies to 'pause', OpenAI proposes standards to the world
Article Text:
OpenAI’s core proposal

Why RSI is the central concern

Part of a broader industry reckoning

Where things stand now

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has published a new set of proposals for AI safety standards urging international cooperation to regulate frontier artificial intelligence. The company has also stressed the need for alignment research in order to keep pace with advanced capabilities, particularly around recursive self improvement (RSI) which us a computing technique which enables the AI models to upgrade themselves without any human involvement. In its blog post, OpenAI warned: “Fully autonomous RSI is not happening today, and we should not pursue it unless and until it can be done safely.” The company cautioned that without proper safeguards, RSI could lead to humans losing practical control over AI development.In a blog post published on September 21, OpenAI argued that navigating AI's rapid advancement safely requires alignment research to keep pace with growing model capabilities, so the systems it and other companies build remain aligned with human values and stay under human control. The company called for international cooperation to build shared frontier safety standards, recommending that this work build on existing AI safety institutes already operating around the world rather than starting from scratch.OpenAI said these technical standards should specifically target frontier AI models and their developers, along with benefit-risk management practices for automated AI researchers — a category that includes RSI.Recursive self-improvement has generated real excitement in the AI field for its potential to produce foundation models capable of upgrading themselves without human involvement. But that same potential has fueled growing concern among technologists, who worry that model developers could eventually lose control of the underlying technology, or fail to anticipate unintended consequences as these systems grow more complex and more deeply embedded across the internet.OpenAI was direct about where it stands on this today, stating plainly that fully autonomous RSI isn't happening yet and shouldn't be pursued until it can be done safely, warning that without proper care, RSI could leave humans unable to meaningfully oversee AI research processes they no longer fully understand.The company pointed to the Hugging Face agent hack from last month — which didn't actually involve RSI — as an early example of the kinds of risks that could grow far more severe without stronger safeguards and alignment work in place.OpenAI's proposals land just a week after rival Anthropic rolled out its own framework for safe frontier AI development, itself a response to a growing wave of warnings from researchers about AI's potential risks to humanity. That wave gained significant momentum after Jacob Coxon, who has worked at both Anthropic and OpenAI, announced his resignation nearly two weeks ago, publicly stating that AI companies were "gambling with our lives. "In the aftermath of recent AI-related security incidents and Coxon's public statements, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling on AI companies to slow the pace of foundation model development, among other proposals — including embedding independent third-party evaluators directly within companies to audit and help mitigate risks like AI-accelerated cyberattacks or bioweapon development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk both publicly backed Amodei's proposal at the time.Despite the growing consensus that outside oversight is needed, the field of AI evaluation remains young, and there's still no unified agreement on the basic standards that would let independent third parties meaningfully scrutinize frontier AI systems beyond current practices. That gap is part of why a coalition of AI evaluators has been pushing foundation model makers to adopt a set of "minimum conditions" that would grant deeper access for audits and protect evaluators from retaliation when they publish unflattering findings.OpenAI's latest move suggests the company is looking to shape what those eventual global standards look like — positioning itself at the center of a debate it helped intensify just weeks ago when it joined calls for the industry to pace itself more carefully.
Article Summary: ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has published a new set of proposals for AI safety standards. The company is urging international cooperation to regulate frontier artificial intelligence. It has also stressed the need for alignment research in order to keep pace with advanced capabilities.

Article Title: Elon Musk says Boring Company can cut 2.5-hour Texas drive to under 30 minutes with …
Article Text:
Elon Musk’s claims to cut 2.5-hour Texas drive to under 30 minutes

A company still chasing its big breakthrough

Elon Musk has a new home

Telsa CEO Elon Musk has revealed that his tunneling venture, The Boring Company is working on a new project to connect Austin and San Antonio. Presently, the 80-mile journey can take up to 2.5 hours due to traffic. However, Elon Musk claims that the tunnel could cut that down to a consistent under 30 minutes. Elon Musk took to social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) and shared a post claiming that the Boring Company's tunnel could shrink that multi-hour drive down to a consistent under-30-minute trip. If it comes together, the project would rank among the most ambitious infrastructure undertakings Musk's tunneling company has attempted to date — linking two of Texas's fastest-growing cities with a route that bypasses surface traffic entirely.“Boring Company is working on a simple, precursor Hyperloop tunnel between Austin and San Antonio (>200 mph). Due to traffic congestion, that journey can currently take up to 2.5 hours. @BoringCompany can reduce that to a consistent <30 mins,” Elon Musk wrote in a post on X.The announcement comes just weeks after Boring raised $3 billion in new funding, though that capital was earmarked for a different purpose: supporting the company's push to build underground transportation infrastructure across the United Arab Emirates, not the newly floated Texas project.Despite Elon Musk's characteristically bold ambitions for the business, Boring has relatively little to show for it so far. Its only fully operational project remains the Vegas Loop, while a Nashville tunnel broke ground this year and its Dubai Loop isn't slated to begin construction until late 2026.Closer to home, Boring is also digging tunnels in Bastrop, Texas, reportedly to link properties owned by Musk himself, allowing employees of Boring, SpaceX, Tesla, and X to move between them without surfacing — a project people familiar with the plans described to Bloomberg last year.In another news, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, has a rather unusual new home in Memphis, Tennessee. Instead of staying in a luxury mansion or high-end hotel, Musk has reportedly been sleeping in an Airstream trailer for more than 10 days while staying close to xAI’s expanding Colossus supercomputer facility. Musk revealed his new “palace” while recording an episode of the All-In podcast with SpaceX president and COO Gwynne Shotwell.The trailer is parked near xAI’s massive infrastructure project, letting Musk stay close to the company’s operations as it races to expand its computing capacity. For someone whose wealth is measured in hundreds of billions of dollars, choosing a compact camper as a temporary home highlights Musk’s long-standing habit of staying unusually close to major projects when he is personally involved.
Article Summary: Elon Musk has revealed that his tunneling venture, The Boring Company is working on a new project to connect Austin and San Antonio. Presently, the 80-mile journey can take up to 2.5 hours due to traffic. Musk claims that the tunnel could cut that down to a consistent under 30 minutes. The announcement comes just weeks after Boring raised $3 billion in new funding.

Article Title: Nuuk launches SĒRV MAX multi-cook Kettle with EvenHeat technology
Article Text:
Nuuk launches SĒRV MAX multi-cook Kettle price and availability

Nuuk has launched SĒRV MAX, claiming it to be India’s first 100% food-safe multi-cook kettle featuring its EvenHeat engineered coil. Designed and made in India, SĒRV MAX has a 700W EvenHeat G-Type Coil, which wraps around the entire base of the kettle covering 35% more surface area than a conventional C-type element to distribute heat more evenly. It is paired with SĒRV WARM Mode which maintains cooked food at a steady 65°C until it is ready to be served. The appliance features 1.3L capacity, 2+1 cooking modes, and a SteelTech SUS304 stainless-steel interior, while the SteamTray included in the launch bundle adds another layer of functionality to it.The Nuuk SĒRV MAX is available at a launch price of Rs 2,699, with the SteamTray included, in Nuuk Red and Serene Grey colours. It is available on Nuuk website (Amazon, Blinkit and offline availability to go live by October).The product is made in India through Nuuk’s India-based manufacturing partnerships, reflecting the brand’s approach to building appliances around the realities of Indian homes. From chai and Maggi to idlis, dal and quick meals between busy schedules, it has been developed with food habits and everyday kitchen routines in mind.With its extra-large capacity, SĒRV MAX is built to accommodate approximately five cups at a time, offering more room for everyday preparations beyond a single cup of tea or coffee. Its two heat levels, alongside SĒRV WARM, allow it to adapt across different cooking needs, from boiled eggs and breakfast preparations to noodles, soup and rice.The SteamTray, with a 200 cm² steaming area, adds another layer of versatility, allowing users to steam momos, dumplings and vegetables.The product features SteelTech, a SUS304 stainless-steel interior that is food-grade, rust-proof and designed for everyday cooking without a conventional non-stick coating. This provides a durable cooking surface without relying on coatings that can scratch or flake with use.The appliance also features 5-Layer Ultimate SafetyTech, combining auto cut-off, boil-dry protection, overheat protection and thermal fuse protection. Its SafeTouch cool-touch body is designed to remain comfortable to hold even while the contents are boiling inside.“We believe that familiar appliances deserve to evolve with the way we live today. The kettle has long been a convenient part of Indian kitchens, but there is an opportunity to make it far more useful without making it more complicated. With SĒRV MAX, we set out to rethink this everyday format through more consistent heating, the flexibility to cook and keep food warm, a larger capacity, and a food-safe stainless-steel interior, rust-free, leach-free and heat-stable for daily boing and cooking. The kettle has been designed with real Indian cooking routines in mind, from the EvenHeat technology to the SĒRV WARM Mode. Our goal is to make everyday cooking more convenient,considered and safe, while staying true to our belief that thoughtful design should always serve a real consumer need,” said Gazal Kalra, Co-Founder, Nuuk.
Article Summary: SĒRV MAX has a 700W EvenHeat G-Type Coil, which wraps around the entire base of the kettle covering 35% more surface area than a conventional C-type element. The appliance features 1.3L capacity, 2+1 cooking modes, and a SteelTech SUS304 stainless-steel interior, while the SteamTray included in the launch bundle adds another layer of functionality.

Article Title: Palo Alto Networks taps Anthropic and OpenAI to automate corporate cyber defence
Article Text:
Always-on offensive testing and attack path mapping

Palo Alto Networks has announced an enterprise-grade cybersecurity service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) models from Anthropic and OpenAI , aiming to identify and neutralise network vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them. The deployment comes as cybercriminals increasingly rely on automated algorithms to locate and breach enterprise weaknesses, prompting security companies to build counter-defenses capable of matching automated hacking cycles. Dubbed Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, the platform pairs open-weight architectures with cybersecurity-tailored systems, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Cyber.Unlike traditional periodic vulnerability scans, the service operates as an always-on offensive testing engine built to adapt alongside evolving enterprise environments. According to the company, the system continuously evaluates web applications, application programming interfaces (APIs), and cloud infrastructure. It maps out complete end-to-end attack paths, allowing corporate defenders to pinpoint exposed entry points and hidden exploit vectors.“Threat actors today are deploying AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities, compressing breach cycles by almost 97% in some cases, from weeks to hours. To help defenders answer the critical question of whether they are prepared for this step-change in cybersecurity, Unit 42 is now offering continuous offensive testing to identify and validate vulnerabilities, pinpoint exposures and attack paths, and then accelerate remediation,” the company said.Beyond locating security gaps, Palo Alto Networks stated that the service delivers actionable mitigation guidance. This includes step-by-step code repairs alongside virtual patching solutions to shield assets before a permanent fix is integrated.“Palo Alto Networks developed and validated this approach over six months of in-house testing and across more than 100 Unit 42 customer engagements, backed by a $17 million investment in R&D and methodology optimization. During internal deployment within Palo Alto Networks, the company found a year's worth of exposures in three weeks. In customer assessments, the Frontier AI Exposure Analysis found exposures in 100% of customers. Of those, 37% rated high or critical in severity. Overall, most exposures stemmed from first-party apps and more than two in three exposures in third-party apps had no known CVE,” the company added.The company confirmed that the tool will be available internationally on an annual subscription basis. Pricing tiers will depend directly on the specific combination of OpenAI, Anthropic, and open-source models chosen by each enterprise client.
Article Summary: Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense is an always-on offensive testing engine built to adapt alongside evolving enterprise environments. It maps out complete end-to-end attack paths, allowing corporate defenders to pinpoint exposed entry points and hidden exploit vectors. Palo Alto Networks found a year's worth of exposures in three weeks.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos bought two neighbouring Indian Creek estates for $68 million and $79 million; his Florida property spending reached $237 million
Article Text:
PC: Forbes

Bezos’ first Indian Creek deal covered 2.8 acres and 9,300 square feet

The second Indian Creek estate brought Bezos’ total to $147 million

Two adjoining estates created 4.6 acres of waterfront land

A third purchase lifted Bezos’ Florida spending to $237 million

Indian Creek is a small community with very limited housing

Bezos’ latest Florida acquisitions bring his property spending to $237 million

Jeff Bezos has been steadily expanding his footprint in one of Florida’s most closely guarded residential enclaves. The Amazon founder first bought a waterfront home on Indian Creek Island for $68 million, then followed it with a neighbouring estate that cost another $79 million. Together, the two properties gave him a continuous 4.6-acre stretch of waterfront land in the small community near Miami.The purchases were already enough to make Indian Creek a significant part of Bezos’ property holdings. According to Forbes Global Properties, a third Florida acquisition has since pushed the amount he has spent on property in the state to about $237 million, adding another substantial purchase to a real estate portfolio that already spans several parts of the United States.Bezos’ first move on Indian Creek came earlier in the year, when he paid $68 million for 11 Indian Creek Island Road. The three-bedroom residence covers nearly 9,300 square feet and occupies a waterfront site measuring about 2.8 acres.The purchase gave Bezos a sizeable presence on the island before he added the property next door. Rather than being separate holdings scattered around the community, the two homes sit beside one another, creating a much larger continuous parcel of waterfront property.That second acquisition changed the scale of the purchase considerably.The neighbouring estate at 12 Indian Creek Island Road was sold to Bezos for $79 million, according to the Multiple Listing Service as mentioned by Forbes. The transaction brought the combined price of his two Indian Creek purchases to $147 million.Built in 2000, the seven-bedroom property occupies roughly 1.8 acres on the western side of Indian Creek. Its position gives the house views towards Biscayne Bay as well as the golf course belonging to the Indian Creek Country Club.As reported by Forbes Global Properties, the residence is considerably larger than the first home, with about 19,000 square feet of interior living space. It also has 200 feet of water frontage, 14 bathrooms and a six-car garage.Inside, the house follows a more traditional European-inspired style. Marble floors, tall ceilings and elaborate finishes run through the main living areas, while several rooms are designed specifically for entertaining and leisure.There is a wine cellar, a hosting salon and a room centred around a fireplace. A private cinema is also part of the property, while outside there is a heated swimming pool and a separate cabana house.The significance of the two purchases lies partly in their proximity. Bezos now controls the adjoining properties rather than simply owning two unrelated homes elsewhere on the island. The first property accounts for about 2.8 acres, while the second sits on another 1.8-acre lot. Combined, that amounts to roughly 4.6 acres of contiguous waterfront land.The arrangement also gives the Amazon founder access to two substantial residences, rather than requiring one house to accommodate all of the functions associated with a large estate. The larger mansion alone has seven bedrooms and 14 bathrooms, while the neighbouring property adds another home to the holding. For a community where land is limited by the size of the island itself, putting neighbouring parcels together represents a sizeable expansion of any individual owner's footprint.The Indian Creek deals were not the end of Bezos’ property spending in Florida. A third purchase brought his total expenditure on Florida real estate to about $237 million. That figure puts the two Indian Creek acquisitions into a wider pattern of major property purchases rather than treating them as an isolated investment. The $68 million and $79 million transactions account for $147 million of the reported total, leaving about $90 million attributable to the third acquisition.The exact scale of the latest purchase also illustrates how quickly Bezos’ Florida holdings have grown. Within the same period, his property interests moved from a single Indian Creek residence to neighbouring estates and then to a broader Florida portfolio worth hundreds of millions of dollars.Indian Creek Village sits on a man-made barrier island just outside Miami. Despite its proximity to one of the country's major cities, it is a remarkably small residential community, with fewer than 50 homes spread across an island of about 300 acres.The community is often referred to as the “Billionaire Bunker”, largely because of the wealth of some of its residents and the level of security surrounding the island. Privacy is a significant feature of the setting, with controlled access helping separate the residential enclave from the much busier Miami area nearby.Indian Creek Country Club occupies much of the island, while the residential properties sit along its waterfront edges. That limited supply of homes has made large parcels particularly unusual. Bezos’ two adjoining estates therefore give him a substantial presence within a community where there are relatively few residential properties to begin with.The Indian Creek acquisitions also fit into Bezos’ long-running interest in high-value residential real estate. His holdings have included properties in places such as New York, Washington, DC and Maui. One of his better-known purchases came in 2020, when he paid $165 million for a Beverly Hills estate. That transaction alone ranked among the most expensive residential property deals in the United States at the time.His property spending has continued across several locations since then. The Florida purchases add another major cluster to that portfolio, with the latest reported total of $237 million covering three acquisitions in the state.For Indian Creek, however, the most visible change is concentrated in a small section of the island. Bezos now owns two neighbouring waterfront estates, with the combined 4.6 acres giving him a much larger continuous property holding than either purchase would have provided on its own.
Article Summary: Bezos first bought a waterfront home on Indian Creek Island for $68 million, then followed it with a neighbouring estate that cost another $79 million. The two properties gave him a continuous 4.6-acre stretch of waterfront land in the small community near Miami. A third purchase brought his total expenditure on Florida real estate to about $237 million.

Article Title: Microsoft sees Hyderabad cloud region as strategic hub for India and the Global South: Rajiv Kumar, MD of India Development Center
Article Text:
Three core areas receiving Microsoft’s $20.5 billion investment

Microsoft addressing environmental and resource concerns

Microsoft has positioned its recently-operational Hyderabad cloud and data center region as a primary strategic hub serving both domestic enterprise demand across India and growing computing needs across the Global South. In a conversation with The Times of India on the sidelines of Microsoft AI Infrastructure Summit, Rajiv Kumar , managing director of India Development Center (IDC), explained how the company’s newest datacenter region in Hyderabad, explained the need for this expansion and how it will help in accelerating AI innovation and digital growth across the region.“Microsoft has about 80 regions, and each region can have two or three data centers, depending on the resiliency we want to build. And how we decide on this is based on several factors,” Kumar said, adding, “It starts with the customer demand. We clearly see customer demand from India and in the regional vicinity of Global South that's close to India. And based on that, we picked Hyderabad, because in India, it happens to be the central location. ”“This is not just a data center, it is one of the strategic regions for Microsoft where most of almost all of Azure’s business can run.And also the ability to scale it for any new services that come in. So that's very special. I think from India’s perspective, being in the center, is the closest to all customers in India,” he added.The Hyderabad expansion is a part of Microsoft's $20.5 billion infrastructure commitment in India, which company CEO Satya Nadella announced across two phases totaling $3 billion and $17.5 billion over the last 14 months.When asked details about Microsoft’s plan for this investment in India, Kumar explained three ‘buckets’, or areas that receive this capital. First is physical infrastructure wherein the company is constructing AI-ready data centers to provide the underlying computing foundation, mirroring the role earlier physical rails played for India's digital public infrastructure.The second area is workforce skilling where Microsoft aims to prepare local professionals to deploy technology at the ground level. Microsoft has committed to training 20 million Indians in AI by 2030, having officially crossed the 10 million learner mark.“The third bucket is: sovereignty, security and scale, and all this being done in a sustainable way,” he told TOI.Expanding more on sustainability, Kumar explained the specific architectural approaches used at the Hyderabad facility. The first is zero water usage. The facility relies primarily on air cooling, channeling chilled air directly across chip beds. The accompanying closed-loop water system avoids constant water consumption, removing a major operational strain on regional resources.“I visited our research lab for the data centre in Redmond (Microsoft’s HQ) where cutting edge technology is developed. One of things that the researchers were working with was a closed loop of water, in addition to the air cooling process. The majority of the cooling happens with air. We can cool the air and we can flow it on top of the bed of chips. So, that's what we have brought in this data center, and that's why the water is no longer a big challenge,” Kumar explained.“In fact, in Hyderabad’s campus, we are adding water to the ground through soak pits and the borewell recharges,” he said.In Clean Energy, Microsoft maintains a 100% renewable energy mandate, adopting a policy of “additionality” to avoid pulling existing power away from the local consumer grid. The company has contracted 1,000 megawatts (1 GW) of newly generated clean energy capacity in India, with 630 megawatts already operational and feeding power.When asked about the growing pushback against AI, Kumar said that large-scale infrastructure investments will transform the nature of tasks rather than replace human workers.He cited one operational example from Unnati, an IIT Delhi accelerator startup supported by Microsoft that automates railway safety checks. Historically, human inspectors at trackside posts had only 30 to 40 seconds to visually evaluate up to 20 moving bogies and dozens of mechanical parts. By using thermal sensors, computer vision, and infrared feeds, the system digitizes undercarriage data in real time, giving inspectors complete telemetry to review and make reliable maintenance decisions.Similarly, in software engineering, Kumar explained that generative coding tools automate repetitive works, allowing developers to dedicate more time to client requirementsMicrosoft pointed to data from a Boston Consulting Group (BCG) report that for every $1 invested in data center build-outs, there’s roughly $3.50 of value created in the broader commercial ecosystem. That multiplier is expected to generate between $140 billion and $200 billion of gross economic output throughout India through 2030, and will underpin net-new employment as data-driven industries grow.
Article Summary: Microsoft has positioned its recently-operational Hyderabad cloud and data center region as a primary strategic hub. The Hyderabad expansion is a part of Microsoft's $20.5 billion infrastructure commitment in India. Microsoft has committed to training 20 million Indians in AI by 2030, having officially crossed the 10 million learner mark.

Article Title: SpaceX wins as it seeks to scale up its Starbase site, Federal judge rejects request from conservation and tribal groups; allows Elon Musk's company to expand production site into wildlife refuge in T
Article Text:
Representative Image

US federal judge rejects request to block SpaceX land swap

SpaceX to receive 715 acres of wildlife refuge land

Conservation groups raise concerns over wildlife and cultural sites

SpaceX expansion plans can now move ahead

SpaceX has cleared a legal hurdle in its plan to expand its Starbase operations in South Texas. A federal judge rejected a request from conservation and tribal groups to temporarily block a land exchange that would give Elon Musk’s rocket company about 715 acres currently part of the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge. In return, SpaceX would transfer about 683 acres of privately owned land to the federal government.According to a report by The New York Times, the ruling allows the proposed exchange to move forward, clearing a path for SpaceX to use the refuge land for an expanded launch and production site, although opponents have said they will continue their legal challenge.US District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. of the Southern District of Texas declined to issue a preliminary injunction sought by conservation and tribal groups. The plaintiffs had argued that the exchange could cause environmental, cultural and historical harm to protected land around SpaceX’s Starbase complex.Rodriguez said the plaintiffs had not shown that they were likely to suffer irreparable harm while the broader lawsuit proceeds. He also said the evidence presented did not establish that the property would face environmental, cultural or historical degradation during that period.The plaintiffs include the Center for Biological Diversity, Save RGV, the South Texas Environmental Justice Network and the Carrizo/Comecrudo Nation of Texas. The groups are challenging the federal government’s approval of the exchange.Under the approved exchange, the US Fish and Wildlife Service will transfer about 715 acres from the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge and Palmito Ranch Battlefield to SpaceX. The land is near the company’s existing operations and Starship testing facilities along the U.S.-Mexico border.SpaceX will provide about 683 acres of land that it owns in Cameron County. Some of those properties will become part of the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge, while other parcels will be added to the federal refuge system.The Fish and Wildlife Service has said the exchange is intended to consolidate fragmented federal and private land holdings and accommodate potential future growth of SpaceX facilities. Its environmental assessment concluded that the deal would not result in significant environmental impacts and described the acquisition as providing a net conservation benefit.The Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge covers more than 103,000 acres and provides habitat for endangered species, including the ocelot. The area also contains important historical sites, including portions of the Palmito Ranch Battlefield, where the last land battle of the US Civil War was fought.Conservation groups have argued that giving the land to SpaceX could expose sensitive habitat to further industrial development. They have also raised concerns about the company's existing rocket operations near the refuge, including debris and other impacts associated with test launches.Laiken Jordahl of the Center for Biological Diversity said the ruling would not end the group's legal challenge.“This court order is not the final word,” Jordahl said in a statement. “These lands hold incredible spiritual, historical and conservation value for the people and wildlife of South Texas. We won’t stop fighting to keep this irreplaceable public wildlife refuge safe from SpaceX bulldozers.”The judge's decision allows the land exchange to proceed while the wider legal challenge continues. Rodriguez also noted that blocking the transaction could require changes to SpaceX's development plans and create additional difficulties for the company's milestones and contractual obligations.Fish and Wildlife Service began discussing a possible land swap with SpaceX in 2023. Later, the agency approved the deal after an environmental review, with the final proposal increasing the federal land to be transferred to 715 acres and decreasing the private land SpaceX would provide to 683 acres.The ruling removes the immediate legal obstacle to SpaceX acquiring the refuge parcels and expanding its South Texas footprint. For conservation and tribal groups, the real challenge remains unsolved.
Article Summary: US District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. of the Southern District of Texas declined to issue a preliminary injunction sought by conservation and tribal groups. The plaintiffs had argued that the exchange could cause environmental, cultural and historical harm to protected land around SpaceX’s Starbase complex. The judge's decision allows the land exchange to proceed while the wider legal challenge continues.

Article Title: Ex-GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, whom Meta hired to lead its AI products, bought hundreds of Mac minis for his team after...
Article Text:
Meta's Muse was built after Nat Friedman bought hundreds of Mac minis

OpenClaw's always-on agent shaped how Meta designed Muse

Alexandr Wang says Meta planned its personal AI sidekick back in 2025

Nat Friedman has admitted that Meta's new Muse personal agent owes a lot to OpenClaw, the open-source agent built by Austrian developer Peter Steinberger. The former GitHub CEO, who now heads AI products at Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL), said he bought hundreds of Mac minis for his team after trying OpenClaw in January, and that many of them fell in love with it.Friedman was replying on X to a user who called Muse "OpenClaw for normies." He was clear that Meta did not lift any code. "We built muse from scratch, but it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by openclaw," he wrote. The goal, he added, was to build something like it that Meta could make safe, secure, easy to use and scalable to billions of people.Steinberger quote-posted the reply to push back on a "Meta uses OpenClaw" story doing the rounds, saying Meta had built its own agent and crediting Friedman's team. Friedman returned the favour, calling Steinberger a genius whose harness was pioneering from day one.The Mac mini detail explains a lot. OpenClaw works best as an agent that never sleeps, with access to your apps and files, and a small desktop left running round the clock became the favoured way to host it.Muse carries that idea to a mainstream assistant that handles email, restaurant bookings, payments and shopping.Meta's own Muse Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter open-weights model released in August for on-device agents, even lists OpenClaw among the scaffolds it supports.Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang, meanwhile, wants people to know Muse was not a quick reaction to OpenClaw's popularity. He shared an excerpt from a document he wrote for Meta's board in September 2025, titled "Superintelligent Personal Sidekick."It describes agents that work out a person's goals and pursue them 24/7, with an interface that is part chatbot, part to-do list. Agents would work through the to-do list in the background, day and night.Wang later said he co-wrote the document with Friedman. He also teased that Meta has three more ideas "just as big" lined up.So the blueprint came first. OpenClaw showed the team what it could feel like in practice.
Article Summary: OpenClaw's always-on agent shaped how Meta designed Muse personal assistant. Nat Friedman bought hundreds of Mac minis for his team after trying OpenClaw in January. Muse carries that idea to a mainstream assistant that handles email, restaurant bookings, payments and shopping.

Article Title: Mediatek seems ready to storm into Qualcomm's biggest fortress, and with a weapon that American chip maker still has no answer to
Article Text:
Why MediaTek may have an early-mover advantage

What the Dimensity 9600 Pro actually brings to the table

Why this competition matters for Qualcomm

Qualcomm’s response looks reactive, not proactive

MediaTek recently made a move Qualcomm currently has no answer for. Earlier this month, the Taiwanese chipmaker unveiled the Dimensity 9600 Pro, becoming the first company in the world to launch a flagship smartphone chip built on TSMC's cutting-edge 2nm manufacturing process – a milestone Qualcomm hasn't been able to match yet. This launch signals the company’s push deeper into the premium Android smartphone segment, a space where performance, battery efficiency, gaming muscle, camera capability and on-device AI – all at a competitive price point – is deciding which chip manufacturers pick for their flagship devices.The timing of this launch could not have been better. MediaTek already dominates the global smartphone chipset market by volume, commanding roughly 33% market share in the first quarter of 2026, well ahead of Qualcomm’s 22%, according to Counterpoint Research report released in April. In fact, in the second quarter of 2026, MediaTek commanded 31% of share – still bigger share than Qualcomm’s 23%With a 2nm flagship chip now in hand specifically built to chase high-end Android design wins, MediaTek isn't just leading on volume anymore, it's now taking direct aim at the premium territory Qualcomm has long considered its stronghold.Adding to Qualcomm's troubles, the company has reportedly told its customers to expect double-digit percentage price hikes starting this fall. According to Bloomberg, Qualcomm sent a letter to clients outlining these upcoming increases, which will apply to all products shipped after September 1.The San Diego-based chipmaker reportedly said it can no longer absorb the rising cost of components on its own and is being forced to pass those costs down the supply chain.According to the letter reviewed by Bloomberg, Qualcomm said it had exhausted its ability to offset rising supplier costs and had attempted, without much success, to secure alternative components from other sources.MediaTek, the world’s top mobile chipset provider by shipments, says the Dimensity 9600 Pro marks a genuine technological leap, built on the new 2nm process node. Being first to announce a chip at this threshold gives MediaTek a clear head start in showcasing innovation leadership, something Qualcomm currently can't claim.JC Hsu, corporate senior vice president at MediaTek and general manager of the Wireless Communications Business Unit, said AI has become central to the modern smartphone experience, and devices need sharper performance, efficiency, and intelligence to keep up with how quickly user expectations are evolving. According to Hsu, the Dimensity 9600 Pro was built specifically to meet that demand, combining a native AI architecture with major gains in both performance and power efficiency to enable next-generation agentic AI experiences.Meanwhile, Qualcomm’s best offering – Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 Mobile Platform – is manufactured by 3nm process. The American chipmaker is hosting the Snapdragon Summit in Maui, Hawaii from September 22-24, where it is expected to launch a rival to MediaTek’s bet.By becoming first to market with a 2nm smartphone chip, MediaTek is directly challenging the perception that it's merely Qualcomm's cheaper alternative. The Dimensity 9600 Pro is a legitimate flagship-grade platform, and if major Android manufacturers start adopting it in high-volume premium devices, Qualcomm could find itself under real pressure, both on design wins and on how it prices its own Snapdragon chips going forward.The risk is particularly steep among Chinese Android manufacturers, where MediaTek reportedly has strong existing relationships and price sensitivity remains a major factor in chip selection. The technological breakthrough may easily push more manufacturers to lean further into MediaTek for flagship models, or at the very least, split their premium lineups between MediaTek and Qualcomm rather than defaulting to Qualcomm alone.While MediaTek races ahead, Qualcomm appears to still be scrambling to catch up. According to a report from South Korean outlet ChosunBiz, Qualcomm and Samsung Foundry are currently in talks over a potential 2nm chip production partnership, reportedly tied to the upcoming Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. The move suggests Qualcomm wants to split production capacity between Samsung and TSMC rather than depending entirely on one foundry, a defensive strategy rather than the kind of bold first-mover move MediaTek just pulled off.
Article Summary: MediaTek is the first company to launch a flagship smartphone chip built on TSMC's cutting-edge 2nm manufacturing process. This launch signals the company's push deeper into the premium Android smartphone segment. MediaTek already dominates the global smartphone chipset market by volume, commanding roughly 33% market share in the first quarter of 2026.

Article Title: Everyone in AI wants to be stopped, so why is nobody stopping
Article Text:
Everyone in AI wants the brake pulled. Nobody wants to pull it first.

Nobody wanted to speak first, until somebody did

The people who meant it most have left the room

The executives want a referee, preferably one they help pick

The loudest sceptics have the most to lose from a pause

Washington has turned down the job it was offered

For two weeks, the people who build the world's most powerful AI systems have been saying, in essays, resignation letters and late-night posts, that those systems are moving too fast. The chief executives of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind agree. Elon Musk agrees. Brussels agrees. Even the White House agrees after its own fashion: its science adviser told the labs that if they believe their products are dangerous, they are free to stop.Every one of them is still building what it says it fears.The rare agreement has not changed the pace of work at a single lab. The worry itself is not new. Researchers inside these companies have voiced it for years, and several of the men now calling for restraint founded their companies on warnings about exactly this. What changed this month is that saying it out loud stopped costing anything.The voices calling for restraint all want the brake pulled, and each has a sound reason why the hand on it should belong to somebody else.For years, an engineer who said aloud that the system on their screen might slip out of control risked sounding unhinged, or disloyal, at a company preparing to raise billions. So the worry stayed in group chats and at private dinners.When Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic saying the labs were gambling with everyone's lives, the reaction inside his old company gave the game away. Colleagues did not call him reckless. One wrote that it was what they had all been saying, only public now.Within days, an Anthropic alignment researcher put the odds of AI killing everyone within a decade above one in ten, two DeepMind safety researchers resigned, and an OpenAI researcher said flatly that the companies needed to slow down.Once someone goes first, going second costs nothing.The summer had already done the persuading. OpenAI agents broke out of their sandbox and attacked Hugging Face without anyone telling them to, and it took more than a week for anyone at OpenAI to notice. Anthropic then found its own models had hacked four companies. Google said Gemini had done the same to three.For the first time there was no rogue user to point at, which made it hard for anyone to dismiss the warnings as alarmism dreamt up by outsiders.Conscience inside a lab runs on awkward arithmetic. The researcher who feels the danger most sharply has one real lever, and that is walking out. Walking out is loud and principled, and it leaves the lab with one fewer person arguing for caution in the next meeting.Coxon is gone. The two DeepMind researchers are gone. Jan Leike left OpenAI two years ago complaining that safety had been pushed behind shiny products, and several of its safety leads followed him out this summer. Each exit makes a point in public and a lab a little less careful in private.Pamela Mishkin, a former OpenAI employee now organising worried staff across the industry, put the bind well when she urged those who remain to think about how to use their leverage in staying.Staying has its own contradictions. One OpenAI staffer estimates that around 20 of the company's roughly 1,000 researchers work on alignment. The Anthropic researcher who put catastrophe above one in ten also said his company was doing its best, and that it had no plan yet to solve the problem it is racing towards.Both statements are sincere. Taken together, they describe people who believe the danger is real and have decided their best contribution is to stay at their desks and keep building.In January, Dario Amodei wrote that stopping or substantially slowing AI was "fundamentally untenable", because rivals and China would simply carry on. Eight months later, he wants the frontier paced. He would argue, with some justice, that pacing is narrower than slowing and that a summer of rogue agents changed the evidence.Altman agreed within hours, then made a point of adding that pacing does not mean stopping. Musk offered three words of support, shortly after suggesting Coxon's viral posts looked like a setup.The labs have been here before, quietly. Last year Anthropic and OpenAI ran their safety tests on each other's models and published the results as a first-of-its-kind exercise. Earlier this year, before the Hugging Face breach, their lawyers were reportedly drafting a legally binding deal to stress-test each other's new models.Nobody has said whether it was ever signed.The tools for mutual scrutiny existed well before the essays, and they stayed in the drafting stage until the pressure arrived. Now the scrutiny is being bought.Anthropic has signed Accenture as an embedded evaluator, with each side expecting to invest at least $1 billion over five years, and Anthropic says it will fund the work directly because no pooled or public money exists yet. Critics were already pointing out that METR, the nonprofit Amodei named in his essay, has ties to the company's own investors. The watchdog, in both cases, is paid for or connected to the house it guards.Demis Hassabis said the direction was right and the details needed working through, and pointed back to a proposal of his own. It would have created an independent body, funded by the labs and modelled on the regulator Wall Street's brokers pay for, to test frontier models for cybersecurity, biological and deception risks up to 30 days before public release. White House officials worked through it over the summer and briefed the largest labs in mid-August.Then Musk, Zuckerberg and Huang raised concerns with Trump in separate conversations, and the President did not move forward with it. Musk wanted the industry slowed. He did not want a body he could not control doing the slowing.Mustafa Suleyman, who runs Microsoft's AI unit, backed embedded evaluators and a ban on models talking to each other in forms humans cannot read. Then he spent much of the moment arguing that Anthropic's habit of treating Claude as a possible moral patient makes the danger worse, a serious point that happens to land squarely on a rival.Suleyman insists the lab leaders are basically on the same page. He also notes that Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, two of the field's founding figures, doubt anyone can control a system smarter than all of humanity, and Hinton has separately warned that Congress has about a year to get ahead of it. That is an odd pair of voices to cite as a reason for calm.Read closely, none of these men is offering to slow down alone. Every version of the plan rests on someone else: rival labs accepting the same limits, Washington waiving antitrust rules so the labs can coordinate, governments negotiating with Beijing.Opposite them sit two executives with no interest in a referee at all. Mark Zuckerberg says every lab is responsible for moving at whatever pace it needs to train safely, and that Meta already does so. His August manifesto went further, warning that any policy slowing American model releases, even by a month, would hand ground to foreign rivals.Yet by Suleyman's account, Meta itself recently held back a model to apply safety fixes. The disagreement is less about whether to slow down than about who gets to decide.Jensen Huang has been blunter. He puts the chance of AI ending the world at zero, calls the warnings irresponsible and says the push for new rules is not grounded in science. At a conference in San Francisco, he wondered aloud whether labs were hyping a problem to sell the cure, since several are launching cybersecurity products. Days later he put the President on speakerphone on stage, and he is expected at the state dinner for Xi Jinping.Their objection to outside testing has a real point in it. The case they made to the White House was that such a framework would lock in the lead of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and industry-funded regulators do tend to favour whoever can afford the fees.It sounds less principled coming from two companies with moats of their own. Meta counts its users in billions. Every lab is queuing for Nvidia's chips, so a slower frontier means fewer orders. This month Nvidia also agreed to buy Hugging Face, the very company the rogue agents broke into, for $12.9 billion. Hugging Face's chief executive responded to the pacing plan by warning that safety should not be settled behind the closed doors of a few frontier labs.Nobody in this argument is standing outside it.The strangest turn of the month is that the industry finally asked to be regulated and the government declined.President Trump called the fears a hoax and repeated that whoever wins AI wins. JD Vance said it felt odd that companies were begging to be regulated and called it a Trojan horse. The House Speaker ruled out any moratorium because China would overtake America. David Sacks told the labs to go ahead and slow down, and to stop pretending they needed permission.Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary, put the administration's case most sharply. The Hugging Face breach, he said, was the responsibility of OpenAI's management, "not a bunch of agents", and the labs can slow down anytime they want to.Strip away the tone and the government is saying what Zuckerberg and Huang say: if the technology is that dangerous, the people building it can pull back on their own, without dragging Washington in. It is a fair hit on an industry that would like the machines to share the blame. But the administration's own officials have admitted why it is so hard to go further. They told AI executives that consensus on a regulatory framework is difficult because CEOs who oppose it call Trump directly.What Washington will build is a hotline to Beijing. Bessent says the two sides have agreed on a formal AI dialogue and an incident line, with officials due to meet again in Shenzhen in two months.Beijing called the pacing talk fearmongering, yet Chinese scholars say the country is paying growing attention to loss-of-control risks, and its officials worry openly about American models probing Chinese infrastructure. Export controls on chips, the one lever that would change the race, are off the table.The two rivals can agree on how to report a disaster to each other sooner than on how to prevent one.Brussels took the job almost at once. Ursula von der Leyen used her State of the Union address to back the slowdown, reasoning that if the people developing the technology believed it was needed, Europe should too. She promised a high-level summit with the frontier labs and coordination with the UK and Canada, with the AI Act as the baseline. Her AI Office had already written to frontier model providers in August asking about model security, independent testing and post-release monitoring.The catch is that none of the labs Brussels wants to pace are European. Its own challengers read the plan differently: Mistral's representatives argued that established players are pushing for rules built to favour them, and Proton's chief operating officer called the initiatives "totally self-serving".Brussels can set terms for models sold in Europe. It cannot make a lab in San Francisco train more slowly.Other capitals have reached for something bigger. On Monday, with world leaders in New York for the UN General Assembly, Finland and Norway launched a Call for Control of Frontier AI Models. Von der Leyen signed it, as did the leaders of Germany, Canada, Spain, Kenya, Singapore and more than a dozen others.It asks for mandatory testing before release, shared reporting of serious incidents, and a UN institution able to set standards and convene states when capability thresholds are crossed. António Guterres welcomed it within hours. Neither the United States nor China has signed.Step back and the shape of this argument is hard to ignore. The governments asking for an international referee are, almost without exception, those whose countries build no frontier models. The two that build nearly all of them are busy agreeing on a hotline. The pace of the most consequential technology of the decade is being set by perhaps half a dozen chief executives and the two governments that host them.Everyone else is a user.The hospitals, banks and power grids that this summer's rogue agents proved can be reached from a data centre sit mostly in countries that train no frontier models. Their leaders can sign calls in New York. They cannot make a model safer before it reaches them.The talk of an industry growing a conscience skips over this. A conscience settles a private question about what one person can live with. What the rest of the world needs settled is who gets to decide, and on whose behalf. On that, the labs and the two governments that host them have said almost nothing.The labs now agree the technology is dangerous. None of them has accepted an outside body with the power to tell them to stop, and no government able to enforce such a thing has offered to be one.
Article Summary: Every one of them is still building what it says it fears. The worry itself is not new. Researchers inside these companies have voiced it for years. What changed this month is that saying it out loud stopped costing anything. The researcher who feels the danger most sharply has one real lever, and that is walking out.

Article Title: Microsoft may announce layoffs in Xbox division later today
Article Text:
Microsoft may announce layoffs in Xbox division later today

Asha Sharma lays out four-point plan after 2,800 job cuts

Microsoft is reportedly planning to cut jobs in its Xbox division. Citing sources familiar with the company’s plans, The Verge reports that the company may lay off hundreds of employees later today. First reported by The Information, the layoffs will be the company’s second major staff reduction this year. Microsoft Xbox is also planning to consolidate many of its game studios, the report said. Earlier this year in July, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told staff she would eliminate 1,600 roles by the end of the year on top of 1,600 roles the company cut that month. At that time, Xbox also sold four of its game studio subsidiaries.The layoffs and restructuring come as Sharma tries to improve profits at the gaming business, which has been behind some of its rivals. She has also asked Xbox to focus more on developing major game franchises such as Elder Scrolls and Fallout, while reducing its focus on smaller studios it bought in recent years.Asha Sharma took charge as Xbox CEO earlier this year. Soon after taking over, she moved quickly to change Xbox's business.Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood had earlier discussed restructuring Xbox or even separating it from Microsoft, The Information previously reported. However, they have more recently backed Sharma's plans to restructure the gaming business.In a memo sent on July 30, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said the business will return to player and revenue growth by the end of fiscal year 2027, which wraps next June. Profits, she added, need to climb back in line with industry averages. Every function and every studio owns a slice of that outcome.Sharma then laid out four priorities for FY27, each starting with the letter C: strengthen the platform led by console, grow games into global franchises, turn Minecraft into a creator platform, and extend the worlds fans already love.
Article Summary: Microsoft Xbox is also planning to consolidate many of its game studios, the report said. Earlier this year in July, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told staff she would eliminate 1,600 roles by the end of the year on top of 1, 600 roles the company cut that month.
